title: Kolli Hills — 70 Hairpins
tagline: Bangalore → Krishnagiri → Salem → Rasipuram → Karavalli → 70 continuous hairpins to Semmedu → Agaya Gangai falls → Namakkal → Dharmapuri → Bangalore. ~620 km over two days to the 'Mountain of Death'.
summary: Kolli Malai in the Eastern Ghats is named for Kolli Paavai, the goddess said to guard the hill with an unforgiving hand — and the ghat road from Karavalli is her handiwork: 70 numbered hairpins in 27 km, stacked on top of each other so tightly the drone shots look fake. On top it's a different world: jackfruit and coffee, the Arapaleeswarar temple, and Agaya Gangai, a 300-foot fall reached by a thousand steps down (and back up). Out via Salem, back via Namakkal so you ride the hairpins once each way and never repeat road.

segments.note: Day 1. Six-lane; leave by 5 AM to clear Hosur before the trucks.
Fast and dull; breakfast at Dharmapuri. Fuel in Salem.
Silk-weaving town; last proper shops before the hill.
Two-lane through paddy to the base of the ghat. Top up here — nothing on the climb.
The 70 hairpins, numbered on stone markers. Bends 15, 21, 35, 52 and 66 are the tight, blind ones. 40–60 minutes if you don't stop; you will stop.

segments.road: Semmedu → Arapaleeswarar temple → Agaya Gangai → down the Senthamangalam side → Namakkal
segments.note: Day 2. Falls are a 1,000-step descent from the temple car park — budget two hours. The Namakkal-side descent is gentler and the road down is better surfaced.
Namakkal fort and the Anjaneyar statue if you want a stop; otherwise the highway north.
Home. Hosur toll traffic after 5 PM is the last obstacle.

highlights: The Karavalli ghat — 70 hairpins in 27 km, the densest sequence of bends in South India, with the plains dropping away behind every third turn.
Agaya Gangai — a 300 ft waterfall in a gorge below the Arapaleeswarar temple; the thousand steps back up are the real workout of the trip.
Seekuparai and Selur Nadu viewpoints — the plateau's edge, 1,000 m straight down to the Namakkal plains.
Vasalurpatty boat house and the Semmedu botanical garden for the lazy afternoon in between.
Namakkal fort on the way home — a hill fort on a single rock in the middle of the town.

offroad.summary: All tarmac, but the ghat is the point. Seventy hairpins on a road that buses, tempo travellers and coffee lorries share; the riding challenge is line discipline, not surface.
notes: Hairpins are tight enough that a bus takes the entire road — stop before the apex if you hear a horn, don't try to squeeze.
Gravel washes onto the inside line at the numbered bends after rain; brake before, not in, the corner.
Fog sits on the top 20 hairpins in the early morning Nov–Jan — headlight on, visibility can drop to 20 m.
Descending the same road is harder than climbing it: engine braking, second gear, and rest the brakes at the viewpoints.
Agaya Gangai steps are steep and wet — trainers in the bag; riding boots will hurt.

timings: Arapaleeswarar temple: 6 AM – 12 PM and 4 – 7 PM. Agaya Gangai path is open 24 hours but do the steps only in daylight.
Boat house 6 AM – 6 PM (₹5, life jackets mandatory). Botanical garden 8 AM – 8 PM (₹20).
No permits or ghat closures; the road is open at night but fog and unlit bends make that a bad idea.
Fuel: Salem, Rasipuram, Sendamangalam, Semmedu (one pump on top), Namakkal. Fill at Rasipuram before the climb.
Stay: TTDC and homestays around Semmedu and Solakadu; book ahead in Dec–Jan.
cautions: The 'Mountain of Death' name is folklore, but the accident record on the ghat is real — mostly overtaking on blind bends. Don't.
Monsoon (Jun–Aug) brings landslides on the Karavalli side; the road has been closed for weeks at a time.
Namakkal-side road (Senthamangalam) is the easier descent if you're tired on day 2.
Day 1 is 290 km plus the ghat; don't attempt it as a one-day return — it has been done, and it's the riders who do that who end up in the folklore.
